subject: Agriculture
title: The DDT Era
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The DDT Era.

hook.text: DDT was hailed as a miracle after World War II. It killed every insect it touched. Then the problems started.

buildup.text: DDT was sprayed on farms, forests, and cities. It controlled malaria mosquitoes and crop pests alike.

discovery.text: DDT accumulated in the food chain—concentrating in predators. Peregrine falcons and bald eagles nearly went extinct.

twist.text: Rachel Carson's 'Silent Spring' in 1962 linked DDT to ecological destruction. The public turned against it.

climax.text: The US banned DDT in 1972. Its legacy launched the modern environmental movement and changed pesticide regulation.

punchline.text: The perfect insecticide was perfectly destructive. One book changed the world.

quiz.question: What book triggered the movement against DDT?

details.summary: DDT was the first widely used synthetic insecticide, hailed as a miracle chemical in the 1940s-60s for controlling malaria mosquitoes and crop pests. Its environmental persistence and bioaccumulation in food chains led to widespread ecological damage and eventual banning in many countries.
details.whyItMatters: The DDT story is a cautionary tale about unintended consequences of chemical pest control. It demonstrated that pesticides can accumulate in ecosystems, inspired the environmental movement, and led to modern pesticide regulation.
takeaways: DDT was widely used from the 1940s-70s to control mosquitoes and crop insects
Its persistence in the environment caused eggshell thinning that nearly wiped out eagles
DDT was banned in the U.S. in 1972 following Rachel Carson's Silent Spring

faq.question: Why was DDT initially considered a miracle chemical?
faq.answer: DDT was cheap, long-lasting, and killed a wide range of insects. It saved millions of lives by controlling malaria-carrying mosquitoes during and after World War II. In agriculture, it dramatically reduced pest damage to crops. Its inventor won the Nobel Prize in 1948.

faq.question: What environmental damage did DDT cause?
faq.answer: DDT persists in the environment for decades and bioaccumulates up food chains. In birds of prey like bald eagles and peregrine falcons, it caused eggshell thinning that brought species near extinction. It contaminated water supplies and accumulated in human breast milk worldwide.
